content: Drug resistance is a frequent challenge in the management of focal epilepsy. This updated review evaluates the efficacy of levetiracetam as an add-on therapy for individuals with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. The original review was published in 2001 and was last updated in 2012. The primary objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness of levetiracetam when used as an adjunctive treatment for patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Register of Studies, MEDLINE, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, up to November 2018. Additionally, manufacturers of levetiracetam and researchers in the field were contacted to identify any ongoing or unpublished trials. The review included randomized, placebo-controlled trials that investigated the use of levetiracetam as an add-on therapy in individuals with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. Two independent reviewers selected the trials, assessed them for bias, extracted data, and evaluated the overall certainty of the evidence. The primary outcomes analyzed included the proportion of participants achieving a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency, treatment withdrawal rates, adverse effects (including behavioral changes), cognitive effects, and quality of life (QoL). The primary analysis was conducted on an intention-to-treat basis, and meta-analyses were performed using the Mantel-Haenszel method to calculate risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), except for adverse effects, which were analyzed with 99% CIs. Heterogeneity was assessed using the Chi² test and the I² statistic. This update incorporated data from 14 trials involving 2,455 participants, most of which had a low risk of bias. Twelve trials included adult participants (2,159 individuals), while two trials focused on children (296 individuals). The doses of levetiracetam tested ranged from 500 mg/day to 4,000 mg/day in adults and 60 mg/kg/day in children, with treatment durations spanning 12 to 24 weeks. When individual doses were analyzed, levetiracetam at 500 mg/day and 4,000 mg/day did not demonstrate significant efficacy compared to placebo in achieving a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency (500 mg: RR 1.60, 95% CI 0.71 to 3.62, P = 0.26; 4,000 mg: RR 1.64, 95% CI 0.59 to 4.57, P = 0.34). However, doses between 1,000 mg/day and 3,000 mg/day were significantly more effective than placebo. When results were pooled across all doses, levetiracetam was significantly more effective than placebo in reducing seizure frequency (RR 2.37, 95% CI 2.02 to 2.78; 14 studies, 2,455 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). A dose-response analysis revealed that for every 1,000 mg increase in levetiracetam dose, the odds of achieving a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency increased by approximately 40% (odds ratio [OR] 1.39, 95% CI 1.23 to 1.58). However, there was notable heterogeneity across several comparisons. Participants receiving levetiracetam were not significantly more likely to discontinue treatment compared to those receiving placebo (pooled RR 1.11, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.40; 13 studies, 2,428 participants; high-certainty evidence). The most common adverse effect was somnolence, which affected 13% of participants and was significantly associated with levetiracetam compared to placebo (pooled RR 1.62, 99% CI 1.19 to 2.20; 13 studies, 2,423 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Behavioral changes were minimal in adults (1% affected; RR 1.79, 99% CI 0.59 to 5.41) but were more pronounced in children, with 23% experiencing behavioral changes (RR 1.90, 99% CI 1.16 to 3.11). Levetiracetam had a positive impact on certain aspects of cognition and quality of life in adults, but it worsened specific behavioral aspects in children. In conclusion, this updated review confirms that levetiracetam, when added to standard care, is more effective than placebo in reducing seizure frequency in both adults and children with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. It is generally well-tolerated, with minimal adverse effects, except for potential behavioral worsening in children. These findings are consistent with the previous review update from 2012. Notably, this review highlights two additional findings: (1) a 500 mg daily dose of levetiracetam is no more effective than placebo in reducing seizures, and (2) the odds of achieving a 50% reduction in seizure frequency increase by nearly 40% for every 1,000 mg increase in levetiracetam dose. Based on these findings, the continued use of levetiracetam in both adults and children with drug-resistant focal epilepsy appears to be justified.
